instruction: none: started by the service for timer
headline: Started by this line's timer to rerun seed 1's step from 5.92 with the newest fix (keeping spheres that detach at a stack's start inside the stack, D0103) under a CPU cap with a log written per handler call, and then to run the frequency 0.4 layer on from 5.29. The log confirms the checker: with that fix seed 1 crawls rather than loops, first through a sphere being rejoined to its stack every 4.45e-10 time units, then through two neighbouring stacks being broken and rebuilt every 1e-14 time units; the frequency 0.4 layer finishes 5.29 and then crawls near 5.292. The first kind of crawl came from the check of pairs inside a stack reacting to round-off; a round-off floor there (D0104) removes it, but seed 1 then stays in the break-and-rebuild cascade, so no layer is past its stuck point yet.

experiments.question: Does seed 1 at frequency 0.3 finish the step from 5.92 to 5.93 with the newest fix, and if not, where does its time go?
experiments.what_was_done: Ran that step from the saved state with a log line written at every handler call and a CPU cap that can interrupt a handler; stopped it by hand at 801 CPU seconds because the machine was loaded and the registered 30-minute cap would have come after the run's end.
experiments.result: It did not finish. For about three minutes one sphere was put back into its stack and pushed out again 97 times, every 4.45e-10 time units. Then two small stacks next to each other were broken by a touch between them and rebuilt, about a thousand times at intervals of 1e-14 time units. That ended after about ten minutes, and the layer had moved only 2e-6 time units past 5.92052 when stopped.
experiments.takeaway: The checker's reading holds: the fix turns seed 1's loop into a crawl in two phases. It is not untested any more.

experiments.question: Does the frequency 0.4 layer get past 5.29 with the newest fix?
experiments.what_was_done: Ran it from the saved state at its old loop instant up to 5.40, with the same log, stopped by hand at 801 CPU seconds.
experiments.result: It finished 5.29 in 240 seconds, exactly as last run, and then crawled: it reached 5.2919 and no further. Spheres were kept and rejoined in bursts, 121 times in all; none was ever released.
experiments.takeaway: The fix gets this layer through one step only; it crawls the same way a little later.

experiments.question: Inside seed 1's rejoin chatter, which contact makes the rejoined sphere pull away again?
experiments.what_was_done: Saved the layer inside the chatter and looked at the contact modes and forces at the next six stack starts, with and without the joining contact.
experiments.result: Each round is the same: the joining contact itself is sliding (its slip is 0.0102) and with it sliding it pulls with a force of -0.079; without it nothing changes mode and the pair opens. My guess that another contact was being pushed past its friction limit was wrong. The rounds are 4.45e-10 apart because the check of pairs inside a stack fires on round-off: the pair's real gap grows by about 1e-20 in that time, far below the noise of a gap computed from positions.
experiments.takeaway: The chatter is a numerical artefact of that check, not physics. This led to the change tested next.

experiments.question: Does a round-off floor in the check of pairs inside a stack stop the crawl?
experiments.what_was_done: Made that check ignore crossings within the same round-off floor the touch search already uses (about 2.5e-14 in gap), and reran both layers with a 900-second cap.
experiments.result: The change acted (the logs first differ at the ninth and eighth handler calls) and the rejoin chatter is gone in seed 1 (3 rejoins against 97 at the same CPU). But seed 1 went straight into the break-and-rebuild cascade of the two neighbouring stacks and stayed in it until the cap, 1380 handler calls, getting less far than without the change. The frequency 0.4 layer still finished 5.29 but took 500 seconds instead of 240, and reached 5.2920.
experiments.takeaway: One cause of crawling is removed; the remaining one is that a touch between spheres of two stacks breaks both stacks, and they re-form and touch again at once. That is what blocks seed 1 now.

questions.question: When a sphere of one moving stack touches a sphere of another at nearly zero approach speed, should the two stacks join into one (as a free sphere joining a stack does), rather than both breaking as now?
questions.why_it_matters: Seed 1 now spends all its time breaking and rebuilding two such stacks every 1e-14 time units (E0126); joining them is the natural fix, but it makes stacks larger and costlier, and it is a choice about how resting contact is modelled.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Next run: trace the approach speed of those touches first; if it is round-off, apply the touch search's round-off rule to pairs between stacks (no modelling change); only if they are real slow touches, join the stacks below the rest speed, recorded as a decision.

questions.question: Still open from earlier runs: should a hit between the rest speed and the wake speed bounce off a stack sphere as if it could not move, or break the stack as now?
questions.why_it_matters: It decides how often stacks are broken, which drives the cost seen in these crawls.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Keep breaking the stack, as built.

proposed_directions.direction: Stop the stack-to-stack break-and-rebuild cascade in seed 1: trace the 93-94 touches (approach speed, whether the stacks are separating), then either treat round-off approaches between stacks as no touch or join the stacks.
proposed_directions.rationale: It is now the only thing seen blocking seed 1 (E0126); the checker flagged the same touches on Nov 27.

proposed_directions.direction: Reconsider keeping detached spheres as stack members (D0103): with the round-off floor in place, test whether simply handing them back free, with the same floor in the touch search, works as well at frequency 0.4.
proposed_directions.rationale: The checker argues D0103 is extra machinery; members were never released in any run, and frequency 0.4 is slower with it plus D0104 than with D0103 alone.

proposed_directions.direction: Make the integrator's start modes consistent with the moment after: a joining contact that slides with large slip (0.0102) and pulls is common in these crawls; a complementarity solve of normal and friction forces at a stack's start would decide in one step whether the sphere joins or leaves.
proposed_directions.rationale: Every loop and crawl of the last three runs passes through a start where the fixed-mode rules disagree with what happens a moment later (E0119, E0121, E0125).

unfinished_runs.reason: Stopped by hand at 801 CPU seconds (registered cap 1800 s): the machine gave each process about 0.6 CPU seconds per wall second, so the cap would have come after the run ended, and local processes do not outlive the run. The result it was registered for (does it finish 5.93) was already settled.
Stopped by hand at 801 CPU seconds for the same reason; it had crawled at 5.2919 for over 300 CPU seconds.

Science otherwise not limited: 75 GB free, data folder 0.83 GB. Sleep could not be checked (pmset and ps are absent on this Linux worker). CPU from the scripts' own process times: E0123 801 s, E0124 801 s, E0125 snapshot 36 s plus diagnostics about 30 s, E0126 900 s twice, tests about 35 s; total about 3500 s, so 0.97 CPU-hours. Scheduled start is the first command's time (the service's start time was not given). (2) The checker's Nov 27 point 1 (E0116's outcome put the inner check's action in the failing step; it came before 5.92) is answered by E0127, a re-analysis registration superseding E0116 with its outcome; no new runs.
